assessmentSummary.identity: A unilateral non-jump landing-position drill: rapidly lower from tall single-leg stance into a controlled single-leg athletic position and hold without hopping or touching the free foot down.
currentCardFindings: The stable movement is a unilateral snap-down and stick, not a cut, sprint stop, or reacceleration drill as implied by generic legacy copy.
The task creates no intentional flight phase; it trains rapid position acquisition, single-leg balance, and eccentric control before hopping progressions.
Controlled taxonomy, anatomy, load, fatigue, environment, and population fields are empty, and the legacy media pool includes bilateral and snap-down-to-jump mismatches.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: every repetition reaches the same depth with stable foot, knee, pelvis, and trunk and no free-foot touch

coachCues: Snap into the landing shape without leaving the floor
Keep the knee over the middle toes
Freeze the pelvis and free foot
athleteInstructions: Drop quickly into a small single-leg squat
Hold for two seconds without hopping

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as the unilateral non-flight snap-down card and remove cutting or reacceleration language. Treat support and cueing as variants, the bilateral snap-down as a regression, and any snap-down followed by a jump or bound as a separate definition.

currentCardSnapshot.description: From a tall stance on one declared leg, rapidly lower without intentional flight into a shallow controlled single-leg athletic position, hold without a hop, step, hand, or free-foot touchdown, then return and reset. One repetition is one same-leg non-flight drop and terminal stick; it excludes a cut, sprint stop, rebound, jump, or bound.

environment.surface: clean dry level non-slip floor with clear one-body-length station
environment.space: one visible unilateral standing station with protected entry and exit
inspection: surface, footwear, clearance, visibility, and stop signal
coach front and side view of foot, knee, pelvis, trunk, free foot, and terminal hold
environment.changeRule: Changing support, laterality, range, surface, cue, rebound, takeoff, hold, dose, symptoms, or substitute requires revalidation.

selectionPrerequisites: pain-free single-leg stance and shallow controlled single-leg squat
understands non-flight drop, same-leg hold, no free-foot touch, stop signal, and reset
safe station and session unilateral lower-body, impact, technical-fatigue, logistics, and duration budgets fit
excludeOrEscalate: pain, giving way, slip, unsafe floor, repeated arch/knee/pelvis/trunk collapse, free-foot touch, rebound, balance loss, or communication conflict
new neurologic, circulation, breathing, chest, balance, or coordination concern
notEstablishedByEvidence: universal range, hold, dose, recovery, readiness threshold, clinical clearance, injury outcome, or performance transfer

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Landing-control exercises must distinguish a non-jump drop, a jump or hop with flight, an elevated drop, and a run-to-stop because approach momentum and drop height change the task.
Single-Leg Snap-Down to Stick must encode takeoff, landing laterality, direction, approach speed, external height, rebound intent, and required hold as identity, variant, or dosage dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
claims: Landing and horizontal deceleration both train force attenuation, but horizontal stopping additionally requires braking impulse to reduce whole-body momentum.
Single-Leg Snap-Down to Stick belongs to landing and braking control; reactive rebounding, maximal jumping, change of direction, and conditioning are separate programming intents.
Force absorption is shared across the foot and ankle, knee, and hip rather than isolated to one joint.

The card should identify plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip abductors and external rotators, and trunk stabilizers with task-specific primary and secondary roles.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
claims: Effective braking coordinates lower-limb flexion, centre-of-mass control, foot placement, and force direction to attenuate and apply braking force.

Observable quality includes quiet controlled contact, whole-foot pressure, coordinated ankle-knee-hip flexion, knee tracking, stable pelvis and trunk, and ownership of the final position without extra steps.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Plyometric and landing intensity changes with speed, external height, body mass, external load, and task complexity.

Exercise difficulty must score technical complexity and physical demand directly, including coordination, impact, supervision, work capacity, and consequence of error; it must not use a skill-library level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
claims: Horizontal deceleration creates high impact peaks, loading rates, and eccentric muscle demand; rapid or repeated exposures can contribute to muscle damage and need volume management.

Single-Leg Snap-Down to Stick needs contact count, approach speed or drop height, laterality, eccentric braking demand, joint and tissue stress, performance-loss criteria, and recovery guidance rather than repetition count alone.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Landing interventions depend on appropriate materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a level non-slip surface, clear landing and run-out zones, stable equipment where applicable, suitable footwear, spacing, coach sightline, and a population-specific readiness screen.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Landing quality and force absorption should be learned before higher-speed, higher-height, repeated, or reactive plyometric work.
Prescribe low-repetition quality sets, landing contacts per side, approach speed or height, hold duration, rest, cue complexity, and progression criteria; stop before fatigue changes mechanics.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Prescriptive instructions and feedback can improve landing mechanics, while excessive or poorly targeted information can interfere with learning.
Use a small cue set: land quietly, share force through ankle-knee-hip flexion, keep knee over the middle toes, control pelvis and trunk, and hold the finish without a touch-down or extra step.
Loud contact, poor stabilization, loss of alignment, or inability to use the ankle, knee, and hip together indicate that intensity or volume exceeds current control.

Stop for pain, giving way, dizziness, repeated valgus or trunk collapse, uncontrolled foot contact, extra steps, loss of the required hold, unsafe surface or spacing, or persistent left-right asymmetry.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence-Based Best-Practice Guidelines for Preventing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Young Female Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
evidence.sourcePublisher: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
claims: Landing stabilization and lower-body strength are recurring components of effective neuromuscular injury-prevention programs.

Single-Leg Snap-Down to Stick belongs after general preparation and before high-intensity jumping, sprinting, or change-of-direction work; rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment require separate clinical context.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Athletes benefit from specific feedback tied to observable landing actions rather than abstract risk language.
Athlete support should show the start and finish positions, state the landing target and hold time, define a successful repetition, provide one primary cue, and explain the stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Coach education and practical implementation affect whether landing interventions can be delivered effectively.

Coach support should provide front and side observation points, pass-fail criteria, contact counting, left-right comparison, regressions, progressions, equipment checks, and rules for reducing speed, height, distance, or laterality.
Beginners should establish landing and stabilization control before progressing from bilateral to unilateral, longer, faster, or shock-loading tasks.

Accessibility can be improved with visual floor targets, demonstrated start and finish shapes, plain-language cues, reduced amplitude, external support, longer holds, and reduced sensory or decision load without assigning an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: In-place landings, jumps covering distance, repeated hops, and elevated or externally loaded tasks have different intensity and programming implications.

Direction, laterality, support, cueing, and low amplitude are usually variants; rebound intent, approach momentum, external height, or a change to testing or return-to-sport purpose may require a distinct definition or contextual profile.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg Drop Squat to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: This describes the same unilateral non-flight rapid lowering and stabilization task.

alternateAssessments.name: Supported Single-Leg Snap-Down
alternateAssessments.rationale: Light external support reduces balance demand while preserving unilateral position acquisition.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive-Cue Single-Leg Snap-Down
alternateAssessments.rationale: An external visual or auditory start cue changes decision demand but not the landing pattern.

alternateAssessments.name: Bilateral Snap-Down to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: Two-leg support is the lower-balance regression with the same non-flight rapid landing-position intent.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg Snap-Down to Jump or Bound
alternateAssessments.rationale: Adding a takeoff after the snap-down changes the primary stimulus to explosive or reactive force production.
